doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: What counts as traditional jazz; favorite trombonists
summary: Mead resists labels and discusses J.J. Johnson, Jimmy Cleveland, Teagarden and George Brunies.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I’m going to ask you about something you said, you said, “We didn’t play or listen to much traditional jazz.” So what is traditional jazz for you?

Well again as I said, I have trouble putting labels on things. Some of the real West Coast Turk Murphy kind of stuff, I guess I never particularly enjoyed that. And I’ve never had much opportunity to play it so maybe if I did I would. But as I say I’m getting more and more blurred as I begin to go back now. Now probably at the moment my two favorite trombonists, after for years being kind of fan of bop trombonists, I mean J.J. Johnson and Jimmy Cleveland were my heroes, and still are, and yet as I listen to Teagarden, I think he’s head and shoulders above anybody, he’s just playing stuff — and now Dick Sherman has got me listening to George Brunies and as I listen to him I think wow. And technically these guys are excellent. This idea that the old musicians weren’t great technicians is crazy. George Brunies is every bit the technician that any of the great bop players are. The most I listen I think good people playing almost anything are fun to listen to.
